title: Social psychology
note: Social psychology studies how other people and the situation shape what we think, feel and do. A recurring lesson is that situations are more powerful than we expect: ordinary people conform, obey and fail to help under the right pressures, while we tend to blame other people's behavior on their character.

read.title: The power of the situation
text: In the 1950s Solomon Asch asked people to match the length of a line, a task with an obvious answer. Each real participant sat with actors who, on some trials, all gave the same wrong answer. About three quarters of participants conformed at least once. The task was clear, so this was mostly normative influence: people went along to avoid standing out. When even one other person broke from the group, conformity dropped sharply.

A decade later Stanley Milgram asked participants to give a 'learner' electric shocks of rising strength whenever he made a mistake. The learner was an actor and no real shocks were delivered, but participants did not know that. About 65 percent continued to the maximum of 450 volts at the experimenter's urging. Obedience fell when the experimenter gave orders by phone or when the learner was close by.

Neither study shows that people are weak or cruel. They show how strongly a situation can shape behavior, more strongly than most of us predict. That is also why we commit the fundamental attribution error, blaming other people's actions on their character while overlooking the pressures they faced.
The lesson is practical. Knowing these pressures exist makes it easier to be the one dissenter, the one who asks a question, or the bystander who steps in.

q.q: Why was conformity in Asch's study mostly normative?
o: The answer was obvious, so people went along to fit in

q.q: What reduced obedience in Milgram's research?
o: The experimenter giving orders by phone
Telling participants the shocks were real

q.q: According to the reading, these studies mainly show that
o: Situations shape behavior more than we expect
